milestones.title: Secure pipeline
build: Mission Control → Learning lab (Git hosting and CI with Forgejo on dev)
proof: A pipeline that blocks a pull request adding a known-vulnerable dependency, and a container image that is signed and ships with an SBOM anyone can verify
careful: Juice Shop is vulnerable on purpose. Run it only on the isolated lab segment, never reachable from the LAN or the internet, and attack only it, your own M6 app and PortSwigger's lab instances, never a site you don't own. The undo is
plain: t
Make the build system check your code and its ingredients for known problems on every change, and stamp what it produces so nobody can swap it later.
why: Attackers increasingly skip your code and go after the build: a poisoned dependency, a leaked CI token, an image swapped after it was tested. On 2026-03-19 it happened to a security scanner: attackers force-pushed 76 of the 77 version tags of Trivy's GitHub Action to an infostealer (

). A workflow that used a tag ran the stealer. One pinned to a commit SHA ran the real code, unless the pinned commit was old enough to fetch setup-trivy by tag, which was hijacked too. So pin every action and tool by commit SHA or digest, and only to a release at least 7 days old: a SHA pin survives a moved tag, and the wait gives a poisoned new release, like Trivy v0.69.4, time to be caught before you take it. A secure pipeline checks code, dependencies and configuration on every change, runs with as little access as possible, and signs what it builds so anyone can check where it came from. Scanners only find what someone taught them to look for, so exploit a bug by hand once, then turn it into a rule. And ship an image that holds only the app and runs with as few rights as possible.
story: "How do you secure a CI/CD pipeline?" A gate that blocked a real CVE before merge, images signed at build and verified at deploy, an SBOM for every build, and the pipeline's own attack surface (runner isolation, pinned actions, scoped tokens) reviewed like application code. "How do you stop SQL injection?" The one you exploited by hand, the Semgrep rule that now blocks it in CI, and the parameterized query that fixed it.

proof: A kube-bench report before and after hardening, admission policies that reject a privileged pod, and a Falco alert for a shell opened inside a container
plain: t
Run containers on a small Kubernetes cluster, set rules that refuse unsafe ones, and get an alert when someone opens a shell inside one.
why: Kubernetes runs many workloads on shared machines, so one badly configured pod can become a foothold on the node underneath. plain: t
Prove you can get everything back after a disaster, and practise what to do if you get hacked, before it happens for real.
why: A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a control. Microsoft's directory for Windows networks. It holds users, computers and groups, checks who is logging on, and pushes settings to every joined machine.
Free, open-source software that answers a network's DNS lookups and refuses names on its blocklists, such as ad, tracking and malware domains.
A Kubernetes gatekeeper that checks every request to create something and can refuse it, for example a container asking for too much power.
Architecture decision record. A one-page note on a choice you made, the options you weighed and why you picked one.
A small, modern tool for encrypting files with a key pair.
A list of addresses or accounts a control never blocks. Keep it short, or it becomes a hole.
A tool that configures many servers the same way from text files, instead of by hand.
A password-like key that lets a program, not a person, use a service. Give each tool its own, with only the access it needs.
A library of small, safe tests that mimic real attacker techniques, used to check whether your detections fire.
MITRE ATT&CK, a public catalogue of the techniques real attackers use, grouped by goal. Used to describe attacks and find gaps in defences.
How much damage one compromised device or account can do. Segmentation and least privilege shrink it.
In CrowdSec, the part that enforces a decision, for example by dropping an attacker's address at the firewall or blocking it at the web server.
A separate line of work in git. You merge it into main when it's ready.
An app letting a user reach data or actions that should be off limits, for example by changing an ID in the URL. The top risk in the OWASP Top 10:2025.
Guessing a password by trying many in a row, usually with a script and a list of common passwords.

Continuous integration. A service that runs your checks automatically on every change.

A standard way to set up a new virtual machine on first boot: users, SSH keys, packages.

A saved snapshot of changes in git, with a message saying why.

A packaged app with everything it needs to run, isolated from other apps but sharing the host's operating system kernel.
A tool that signs container images and checks those signatures before they run.
Getting a website to run an attacker's script in another visitor's browser, for example through a comment or a crafted link. Written XSS for short.
An open-source security engine. It reads logs, spots attack behaviour such as an SSH brute force, and tells bouncers to block the attacker.
Capture the flag. A security game: you break into a test system and prove it by finding a hidden code, the flag. OverTheWire, VulnHub and Hack The Box all work this way.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. A public ID for a known security bug, such as CVE-2026-33634.
Dynamic application security testing. Attacking a running app from the outside to find weaknesses.
A rule style where everything is blocked unless a rule explicitly allows it.
Several independent layers of protection, so one failure doesn't mean a breach.
A rule that turns a suspicious event in your logs into an alert someone sees.
DomainKeys Identified Mail. A signature a sending mail server adds, so the receiver can check the message really came from that domain and wasn't changed.
A domain's published rule for what receivers should do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM checks: deliver it, quarantine it or reject it.
The internet's phone book. It turns names like example.com into addresses computers can use.
When the real system no longer matches what your code or documents say it should be.

A device or program that decides which network traffic is allowed through, based on rules.

Removing what a system doesn't need and locking down what's left, so there's less to attack.

Safe to run again. A second run changes nothing because everything is already as described.

A request to merge a branch. It's where checks run and reviews happen.

An AWS setting that stops storage buckets from being made public, even by mistake.
Static application security testing. Reading source code for security bugs without running it.

Anything that grants access: a password, an API token, a private key.

Splitting a network into zones, so a problem in one zone can't spread freely to the others.

Slipping database commands into a form field or URL, so a badly written app runs them against its own database.

Talking through an incident scenario step by step, without touching real systems, to find gaps in your plan.

A command-line tool for packet capture.

Terraform's record of what it built. It can contain secrets, so it must be protected.

A scanner that finds security problems in GitHub Actions workflow files.

lesson: A tag can be moved to point at malicious code, as happened to
in March 2026. A full commit SHA can't move.
